params.question: A mildly raised tumour marker in a patient with non-specific symptoms is reliable evidence of an underlying malignancy.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: A mildly raised tumour marker is not reliable evidence of malignancy. The opening case illustrated this: CA 19-9 was mildly elevated, yet CT, PET, and endoscopy were all normal. In patients without strong clinical suspicion, tumour markers produce frequent false positives and are intended for monitoring known cancers, not for screening.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct. As the opening case showed, a mildly raised CA 19-9 triggered extensive investigation — CT, PET, and endoscopy — all of which were normal. Tumour markers lack the specificity to serve as screening tools in low-risk patients, and a mildly raised result is far more likely to trigger a harmful cascade of follow-up tests than to identify true cancer.

params.question: A D-dimer test is positive in a young, healthy individual with no risk factors for thromboembolism. Why is this positive result less trustworthy than the same result in a post-surgical patient?

answers.text: The sensitivity of D-dimer decreases in younger patients

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Sensitivity is a stable property of the test itself and does not change with the patient's age or setting. The issue lies with how pretest probability affects the meaning of a positive result.

answers.text: Low pretest probability reduces the positive predictive value of the test

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: When pretest probability is low, even a reasonably specific test produces many false positives relative to true positives, reducing the positive predictive value. The same positive result becomes far more informative when the clinical setting raises the prior probability of disease.

answers.text: Specificity is higher in hospitalised patients than in outpatients

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Specificity, like sensitivity, is a property of the test and does not vary with the clinical setting. It is the predictive values — PPV and NPV — that shift with pretest probability.

answers.text: Negative predictive value is the only metric affected by the clinical context

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Both positive predictive value and negative predictive value shift with pretest probability. A low pretest probability inflates NPV but deflates PPV, which is precisely why a positive result in a low-risk patient is less trustworthy.

overallFeedback.feedback: The key principle is that positive predictive value falls when pretest probability is low. Sensitivity and specificity are stable properties of the test, but the predictive values shift with the clinical context. A positive result in a low-risk patient is far more likely to be a false positive.
Exactly. Pretest probability is the missing variable that turns the same test result into either a genuine alarm or a false trail — always estimate it before you order the test.

interactions.label: A 62-year-old man presents with painless obstructive jaundice and weight loss. U

params.question: A 62-year-old man presents with painless obstructive jaundice and weight loss. Ultrasound confirms bile duct dilatation. What is the most appropriate next investigation?

answers.text: Measure CA 19-9 and reassure the patient if the level is normal

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: A normal CA 19-9 does not exclude pancreatic malignancy. Tumour markers support the clinical picture and are tracked as trends — they cannot replace imaging for staging or tissue diagnosis for confirmation.

answers.text: Repeat the ultrasound in six weeks to confirm the finding

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Delaying investigation in a patient with a high pretest probability of malignancy risks allowing disease progression. The clinical picture demands prompt staging, not watchful waiting.

answers.text: Contrast-enhanced CT abdomen to assess local extent and staging

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: After ultrasound confirms biliary obstruction, contrast-enhanced CT addresses the next clinical questions: local extent, nodal involvement, and distant metastases. This follows the investigation sequence of clinical question → pretest probability → least-risk modality that changes management.
Exploratory surgery without prior imaging and tissue diagnosis exposes the patient to unnecessary operative risk. Non-invasive staging should precede any surgical intervention.

overallFeedback.feedback: After ultrasound confirms obstruction, contrast-enhanced CT is the appropriate next step to stage the disease — assessing local extent, lymph node involvement, and distant spread before proceeding to tissue biopsy.
Correct. The investigation sequence moves from biochemical baseline to ultrasound, then to CT for staging, then to biopsy for tissue diagnosis — each step answering a specific clinical question.

interactions.label: What is the key biological distinction between carcinoma in situ and invasive ca

params.question: What is the key biological distinction between carcinoma in situ and invasive carcinoma?

answers.text: Carcinoma in situ involves well-differentiated cells, whereas invasive carcinoma is always poorly differentiated

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The degree of cellular differentiation (tumour grade) is independent of whether the cancer has invaded. Both well- and poorly-differentiated cancers can be either in situ or invasive — the distinction depends solely on the basement membrane.

answers.text: Carcinoma in situ can spread to regional lymph nodes but not to distant organs

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Carcinoma in situ cannot spread at all. Because the malignant cells remain confined above the basement membrane, they have no access to lymphatic or vascular channels.

answers.text: In carcinoma in situ, malignant cells have not yet breached the basement membrane

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The basement membrane is the critical structural boundary. Malignant cells confined above it cannot access lymphatic or vascular channels, so metastasis is impossible. Only once this membrane is breached does the lesion become invasive and capable of spreading.

answers.text: Invasive carcinoma develops without a preceding dysplastic stage

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Most invasive carcinomas evolve through a recognised sequence: normal epithelium → dysplasia → carcinoma in situ → invasive carcinoma. The colon's adenoma-carcinoma sequence is the classic example of this stepwise progression.

overallFeedback.feedback: The defining distinction is the basement membrane. In carcinoma in situ, malignant cells are confined above this membrane and cannot access lymphatics or blood vessels. Breaching the membrane marks the transition to invasive carcinoma and the possibility of metastasis.

Exactly. The basement membrane is the biological threshold separating curable pre-invasive disease from potentially metastatic cancer — and the reason detecting disease before invasion can prevent spread entirely.

interactions.label: A cancer is detected at an early stage, confined to its organ of origin, and pre

params.question: A cancer is detected at an early stage, confined to its organ of origin, and presented to the multidisciplinary tumour board. Which treatment implication most directly follows from the early stage at diagnosis?

answers.text: The tumour board discussion can be omitted since early-stage cases are straightforward

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Every cancer benefits from multidisciplinary input. The tumour board ensures that the treatment plan is coordinated and evidence-based, regardless of stage.

answers.text: Combined chemotherapy and radiotherapy must precede any surgical intervention

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Neoadjuvant combined treatment is not mandatory for early-stage disease. The advantage of early detection is precisely that less intensive treatment — potentially surgery alone — may be curative.

answers.text: Surgery alone may be sufficient for cure

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: When cancer is confined to its organ of origin, the multidisciplinary team often has curative options including surgery alone. Advanced-stage disease, by contrast, typically requires combined modalities or may only permit palliative care. This is the fundamental reason earlier detection improves outcomes.

answers.text: The pathologist's contribution becomes unnecessary in early-stage cases

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The pathologist provides the tissue diagnosis and histological details — grade, margins, molecular markers — that guide the team's treatment decision, regardless of stage.

overallFeedback.feedback: The key advantage of early-stage detection is that the multidisciplinary team has more treatment options, including potentially curative surgery alone. Advanced disease narrows those options to combined modalities or palliation — which is why detection timing is one of the few modifiable levers on cancer mortality.

Correct. Earlier detection shifts the stage curve, giving the multidisciplinary team curative options — often surgery alone — that are no longer available once cancer has spread beyond its organ of origin.
